Process_Text.original: Binder jetting specimens were fabricated by the ExOne Company using an M-Flex system with an ethylene glycol monobutyl ether (aqueous-based) binder. Green body products were sintered utilizing a sintering profile that reached maximum temperatures of 1310 °C (with a dwell time of 2 h), taking roughly 16 h total until cooldown. All as-fabricated cylindrical samples underwent post-fabrication hot isostatic pressing (HIPing) for 3 h at 1163°C ± 3.5°C and 102 MPa ± 1.72 MPa.
Process_Text.simplified: Binder jetting (ExOne M-Flex) → curing (195 °C, ~1 h per 10 mm part height) → sintering (1310 °C peak, 2 h dwell, ~16 h total) → HIP (1163 °C, 3 h, 102 MPa) → machining

Structure_Text.original: Samples produced through binder jetting showed a consistent microstructure regardless of build orientation, with an amount of porosity present in both microstructural directions. Larger grains are evident with an average grain diameter of 57 μm. The micrographs also revealed annealed twins within the austenitic grains.
Structure_Text.simplified: HIPed binder jetting Inconel 625: equiaxed grains with annealed twins, porosity present, avg grain diameter 57 μm

Process_Text.original: EPBF specimens were printed using an Arcam A2 system with optimized parameters developed in-house for which density was the success metric. Parameters included a powder bed preheat temperature target of ~850 °C, a beam speed of 500 mm/s, an average current of 14 mA, and a focus offset of 20 mA. All as-fabricated cylindrical samples underwent post-fabrication hot isostatic pressing (HIPing) for 3 h at 1163°C ± 3.5°C and 102 MPa ± 1.72 MPa. EPBF and LPBF specimens were cut from the start plate using a band saw before HIPing.
Process_Text.simplified: EPBF (Arcam A2) → cut from substrate → HIP (1163 °C, 3 h, 102 MPa) → machining

Structure_Text.original: EPBF fabricated components have distinct characteristics that appear to be dependent on build orientation. Parallel to the build direction, grains have a more uniform pattern. Perpendicular to the build direction, the microstructure appears with a textured columnar grain morphology, with grains measuring an average of 16 μm wide and 356 μm in length. The dark linear areas are columns of γ'' precipitates following the build direction. After HIPing, equiaxed grains and annealing twins formed (per Amato et al., 2012).
Structure_Text.simplified: HIPed EPBF Inconel 625: columnar grain morphology (avg 16 μm wide, 356 μm long) → HIP transforms to equiaxed grains with annealing twins (Amato et al., 2012); γ'' precipitates in columnar pattern (this work)

Secondary_Phases.Morphology: Disk platelets, columnar array pattern parallel to build direction

Grain_Size.Note: Grain morphology is build-orientation dependent; after HIPing, equiaxed grains and annealing twins form (per Amato et al., 2012)

Process_Text.original: LPBF parts were fabricated in an SLM Solutions 125 HL system available in-house using commercially available parameters specifically developed by SLM Solutions GmbH for processing the Inconel 625 alloy at 30 μm layers. These parameters consisted of a power of 175 W, laser speed of 600 mm/s, and hatching space of 0.14 mm. All as-fabricated cylindrical samples underwent post-fabrication hot isostatic pressing (HIPing) for 3 h at 1163°C ± 3.5°C and 102 MPa ± 1.72 MPa. EPBF and LPBF specimens were cut from the start plate using a band saw before HIPing.
Process_Text.simplified: LPBF (SLM Solutions 125 HL, 175 W, 600 mm/s, 0.14 mm hatch, 30 μm layers) → cut from substrate → HIP (1163 °C, 3 h, 102 MPa) → machining

Structure_Text.original: The microstructure of LPBF fabricated parts appears homogenous and with equiaxed grains compared to those of produced by EPBF and binder jetting in both studied orientations. The average grain size using the line intercept method for this material was 27 μm, a 53% decrease in size from that of binder jetting.
Structure_Text.simplified: HIPed LPBF Inconel 625: homogenous equiaxed grains, avg grain size 27 μm; most similar to wrought Inconel 625 non-annealed state
